THOUGHT: The presenting vaginal bleeding in an 18-month-old plus bilateral breast enlargement indicates precocious estrogen effect rather than local trauma or coagulopathy (no easy bruising, normal external genitalia, intact hymen). The lack of pubic hair favors peripheral (gonadotropin-independent) precocious puberty. The presence of multiple café-au-lait macules and focal lytic/sclerotic bone lesions with leg pain/limp strongly suggests fibrous dysplasia. The classic triad of peripheral precocious puberty, café-au-lait spots, and polyostotic fibrous dysplasia is diagnostic of McCune–Albright syndrome (a postzygotic activating GNAS mutation). Radiographic “patchy lytic and sclerotic” femoral metaphyseal lesions are characteristic of fibrous dysplasia and explain the bone pain/previous fracture risk. Sexual abuse is unlikely given intact hymen and concordant endocrine findings. CBC and electrolytes are normal, which does not suggest hematologic or metabolic causes. Therefore the constellation of findings most likely represents McCune–Albright syndrome with peripheral precocious puberty from ovarian estrogen-secreting cyst(s) and fibrous dysplasia causing the bony lesions and limp.

DIAGNOSIS: McCune–Albright syndrome (polyostotic fibrous dysplasia with peripheral precocious puberty).
